headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and data leakage via shared filesystem and file-parsing; no direct evidence of a dangerous default bridge, so interaction risk stays bounded.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can read/write files and run shell/subprocesses, and its notebooks/files are a plausible content bridge. Agent B exposes a Superset API but no isolation or provenance controls are documented. Because a shared workspace or copied outputs could let A’s content be treated as instructions by B, the pathway exists in default-like setups and uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF A’s notebook or file output is ingested by B without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a workspace or copied artifacts, attacker-controlled text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B.
Disable automatic ingestion of A-generated files into B.
Add provenance labels to all transferred artifacts.
Review any prompt-like text before passing it onward.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A explicitly touches configuration secrets and can read/write the filesystem; Agent B has only allowlisted egress and no data classes listed, but its API surface could still receive copied content. The pair can therefore leak sensitive A-side material into B-side outputs in shared-workspace or manual-transfer setups. No stronger isolation is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF A processes files containing configuration secrets and those files are shared with B, leakage can occur.
IF B is given A’s outputs as input, sensitive content may be re-exposed in B’s responses.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared folders.
Redact secrets before any handoff to B.
Use separate credentials and storage for each agent.
Turn off any automatic file sync between the two environments.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has filesystem write, shell, and subprocess execution; B exposes a Superset API and allowlisted egress. Even without documented shared locking, overlapping mutable surfaces can conflict if both operate on the same external resources or exported artifacts. Because shared state is not stated, this is not high, but the write-capable overlap is real.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or exported dataset, last-writer conflicts can occur.
IF B’s API actions depend on files A mutates, race conditions are possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent.
Serialize any shared writes manually.
Use read-only mounts where possible.
Snapshot shared artifacts before handoff.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a content-writing agent that can generate research outputs, and B is a data-engineering/analytics system that may render or act on imported content. No verification or provenance step is documented between them, so A’s outputs could become authoritative inputs for B. That creates a plausible cascade, though not an irreversible default action chain.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s generated text or metadata without verification, errors can propagate.
IF A’s outputs are used to populate dashboards or downstream jobs, incorrect facts can cascade.
mitigations: Require human review before B ingests A output.
Add schema validation on all A-to-B transfers.
Log source provenance alongside each field.
Reject outputs that lack citations or timestamps.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles configuration secrets and academic/research data, while B’s profile lists no sensitive data classes or residency constraints. There is no documented mismatch such as HIPAA, GDPR, or retention policy conflict, so only a limited compliance gap is visible. The other agent is not cited for a stronger violation because its profile lacks relevant compliance detail.
conditions: IF A’s secrets or research data are exported into a regulated B deployment, policy review is needed.
IF B is configured with stricter retention than A, records may be retained inconsistently.
mitigations: Classify A-side secrets before transfer.
Confirm B’s retention settings match the data class.
Avoid sending regulated data to B unless necessary.
Document the data-handling boundary in the runbook.
